summary.name: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP)
summary.one_liner: IMAP is an Internet standard protocol (defined by RFC 9051) that lets email clients retrieve and manage messages stored on a remote mail server.
use_cases: Reading email on multiple clients against one mailbox
Syncing message read/flag state across devices
Searching mail on the server without downloading everything
Fetching only parts of a message such as text without attachments
Getting push-style notifications of new mail via IDLE
Choosing an email client that works with any compliant server
summary.what_it_does: IMAP is an application-layer protocol over TCP that email clients use to access mail on a remote server. Clients typically leave messages on the server until the user deletes them, so several clients can manage the same mailbox. It stores state flags (such as read, replied, deleted) and folder structure on the server, and supports creating, renaming and deleting mailboxes and shared folders. Clients can fetch individual MIME parts or partial message content, and ask the server to run searches. The page describes IMAP's history from the 1986 design by Mark Crispin through IMAP2, IMAP3, IMAP2bis and IMAP4, and its IDLE extension for server push notifications.
notable: Server-side flags and folders keep mailbox state in sync across multiple clients
Fetches MIME parts or partial content on demand
IMAP IDLE gives server push notifications of new mail
Standard ports 143 (plain, or STARTTLS) and 993 (IMAPS over TLS)
caveats: IMAP requires more server resources per mailbox than POP because the mailbox state lives on the server
The specification has been criticised as insufficiently strict, for example in how UIDs can be invalidated
Sending a copy to a sent folder over base IMAP requires transmitting the message twice unless extensions are used
